Getting started

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

shinyOAuthDB helps you build Shiny apps that query a database or data platform using each app user’s own account. People sign in with the account they already use for that data source, and your app queries data on their behalf.

This is useful when your organization already manages data permissions in the database. For example, if an analyst can only read sales for their region, your Shiny app can use the same restriction. You keep those access rules in the database rather than maintaining another set in the app.

How sign-in and data access work

shinyOAuthDB works with shinyOAuth, which handles the browser sign-in and token renewal. shinyOAuthDB connects that sign-in to your database queries or API calls:

  1. Your Shiny app sends the user to a sign-in service, such as Microsoft Entra, Google, or Keycloak. This service is the OAuth provider.
  2. The user signs in and, if asked, approves the access your app requests. They enter their password with the provider; your app doesn’t collect it.
  3. The browser returns to your Shiny app. shinyOAuth obtains an access token, a temporary credential for making requests on that user’s behalf.
  4. shinyOAuthDB supplies that token when opening a database connection or making an API request. The data source checks it and applies the user’s permissions.

The data source must be configured to accept tokens from that provider. Signing in successfully doesn’t give someone access to a database or table; they also need the relevant database permissions.

Install

Installing from GitHub builds the package from source. Install the build tools for your R version first:

  • Windows: Rtools matching your R version.
  • macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools, installed with xcode-select --install in Terminal.
  • Linux: your distribution’s R development package and C build tools; for example, r-base-dev and build-essential on Debian or Ubuntu.

These tools are needed even for HTTP backends that do not need a database driver.

if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("remotes")
}
remotes::install_github("lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB")

This also installs shinyOAuth. Some data sources need an additional R package or database driver; their guides list the requirements. Add build_vignettes = TRUE to the installation call if you want to read the guides locally with vignette().

Build a small app

The README’s example reads a PostgreSQL table through PostgREST, an HTTP API for PostgreSQL. It runs Shiny in your R session and starts the database and Keycloak sign-in service in Docker. You don’t need a cloud account or a database driver.

Install and start Docker with Linux containers and Docker Compose 2.24.4 or later. Also install jsonlite in R for the API responses:

install.packages("jsonlite")

Save the following as example.R and run source("example.R"):

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

# Start PostgreSQL, PostgREST and Keycloak in Docker
demo <- oauth_db_demo("postgrest", action = "services")

client <- oauth_client(
  demo$provider,
  client_id = "shiny-db",
  client_secret = "demo-client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:18100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "database.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  postgres <- oauth_db_postgrest_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = demo$url
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    postgres$select("visible_rows", order = "row_id.asc")
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(
    ui, server,
    uiPattern = ".*",
    onStart = function() { onStop(demo$stop) }
  ),
  port = 18100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

The first Docker build takes a few minutes and needs internet access and several GB of disk space. When Shiny is ready, open http://localhost:18100 in your regular browser. Embedded RStudio/Positron viewers can’t complete the sign-in redirects. Your browser may ask you to accept Keycloak’s generated local test certificate.

Sign in as alice with password alice. The table shows alice-visible-1 and alice-visible-2. Sign out, then sign in as bob with password bob: you’ll see Bob’s rows instead. The app sends the same request for both users; PostgreSQL’s row policies determine the result.

Stop the Shiny app to remove the Docker services and sample data. The onStop(demo$stop) call arranges this cleanup. If you start the services separately, call demo$stop() when finished. These accounts and the client secret are public demo settings; use your own registration for a real app.

What each part of the app does

client holds the settings for your app’s OAuth registration: where users sign in, the app’s identity, and the access it requests. Create it outside server(), since every visitor uses the same registration.

oauth_ui() wraps your Shiny UI so shinyOAuth can handle the browser’s return from sign-in. Its id = "auth" matches the ID passed to oauth_module_server(); uiPattern = ".*" lets Shiny serve the callback paths too.

Inside server(), oauth_module_server() manages sign-in for that visitor’s Shiny session. With auto_redirect = FALSE, the app waits for the Sign in button. The two observers connect the buttons to auth$request_login() and auth$logout().

auth$connection is a function that provides the current authorization. Pass the function, without parentheses, to oauth_db_postgrest_api() so the API client can check it each time it needs a token. Create this helper inside server() to keep it with the visitor who signed in.

Finally, $select() reads the table and returns a data frame for renderTable(). Before sign-in, the helper waits quietly, like shiny::req(). Because the call runs inside a reactive output, Shiny updates the table when the authorization changes and clears it on sign-out. See ?oauth_db_postgrest_api for filters and other request methods.

Connect your own data

Choose your source

Each guide has the source’s setup requirements and a complete app. You can keep the same sign-in/UI pattern and replace the demo’s provider, client settings and data helper with the ones in your guide.

See Recorded backend checks for tested versions and the parts of each integration that still need deployment validation.

Data source Setup guide
PostgreSQL Native OAuth, PostgREST, Supabase, Azure PostgreSQL
SQL Server Azure SQL and SQL Server
CockroachDB CockroachDB
MySQL Azure Database for MySQL
Cloud data platforms Fabric and Power BI, Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
Query engines Trino and Starburst, StarRocks, SingleStore, ClickHouse, DuckDB over Quack
Other databases and APIs libSQL and Turso, CrateDB, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, SAP HANA, Oracle Database, Oracle REST Data Services, Salesforce

Register your app

An OAuth app registration tells the provider which application is asking for access. Create one, or ask your administrator for one, using the instructions in your source guide. These are the settings you’ll encounter:

Setting What it means
Client ID The provider’s identifier for your app
Client secret Your app’s credential, kept on the Shiny server; some registrations don’t use one
Redirect URI The exact address where the browser returns after sign-in
Issuer The URL identifying the service that issues the tokens
Scopes Permissions your app requests during sign-in
Audience The database or API the access token is intended for

Most source guides use http://localhost:8100 as the redirect URI; the Docker example above uses http://localhost:18100. Register the exact address, including any path and trailing slash, and run Shiny on the same port. When deploying, register your app’s HTTPS address.

For a self-hosted provider such as Keycloak, follow its app registration instructions and your source guide. The database must trust that provider and accept its tokens. Use an access token intended for the data source; an ID token describes the login and serves a different purpose.

Save credentials and run the app

Open your app project’s environment file with file.edit(".Renviron") and add the values requested by your source guide, for example:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret

Keep .Renviron out of Git and restart R after editing it. The source examples read these values with Sys.getenv(). On a hosting service, set the variables in the app’s environment settings.

Copy your source guide’s app into example.R, replace its connection settings, and run source("example.R"). Open the registered address in a regular browser. If sign-in works but a query fails, check the token’s audience and scopes, the user’s database grants, and network access from the Shiny server to the data source. Keep tokens and secrets out of logs.

Query with DBI or dbplyr

DBI is R’s common interface for sending SQL queries to a database and reading the results. dbplyr lets you write queries with dplyr functions; it translates them to SQL for the database to run.

For sources that support DBI, the helper returns a reactive function, usually called con. For example, inside server() in an Azure SQL app:

con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  auth$connection,
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting"
)

output$rows <- renderTable({
  connection <- con()
  DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT TOP (10) * FROM sales")
})

Call con() inside each render or reactive expression that queries data. It checks the current authorization and reuses the visitor’s connection when possible. For dbplyr, pass connection to dplyr::tbl() and use dplyr::collect() when you need a data frame.

Other sources provide API clients: BigQuery has $query(), while Fabric and Databricks can call functions from their supporting R packages through $call(). The source guide and helper’s function help describe the methods.

More ways to try an app

oauth_db_demo() runs a complete local app in Docker, including its R packages and drivers. Use oauth_db_demo("postgrest", app = "local") for an editable app running in local R with its services in Docker. That mode also needs callr and bslib (0.9.0 or later). Run one demo at a time, since they share ports. See ?oauth_db_demo for supported databases, copying files with action = "files", and recovery with action = "stop".

For a cloud workspace, oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks") guides setup in the R console and launches an editable local app without Docker. It also supports Fabric, BigQuery, Snowflake, Azure SQL, Azure PostgreSQL, Redshift and ClickHouse; their source guides list the requirements. Enter ? for help or cancel to save an incomplete setup. The launcher prints a command to resume it. Edit the copied app.R, save and reload the browser to change the query.

Cloud demos use real accounts and existing resources. Queries can consume compute or query allowances; stopping the demo ends the local app while shared cloud services keep running. See ?oauth_db_cloud_demo for offline drafts, saved settings and script arguments.

Sessions, saved results and extra permissions

Keep connections and API clients inside server(). On sign-out, account changes or session end, the helpers stop providing the old connection and call its cleanup method. Driver behavior varies, so call con() before each operation instead of keeping a native connection or copied token for later use. shinyOAuth handles token renewal. See ?oauth_db_connect for token lifetime and connection options.

Longer queries

The built-in HTTP query methods and ordinary DBI queries run synchronously. While a query, result download or polling loop waits, it can delay other Shiny sessions in the same R process. For HTTP clients, set timeout to suit the operation; the helper’s help explains whether it covers one request or the full operation.

Keep live connections and token callbacks in the Shiny session that created them. For background work, use the database package’s supported approach and check the current authorization before displaying a result. Signing out doesn’t necessarily cancel work already submitted to a platform.

Save query results

Closing a connection doesn’t erase data you’ve already fetched. If you store results in reactiveVal(), eventReactive() or a cache, clear or hide them on sign-out, account changes and loss of required permissions. A shared cache keyed only by SQL can expose one user’s results to another. The source checkout’s playground/example-query-button.R shows a query button that clears saved results when access changes.

Use an existing login or several accounts

The *_client() functions are optional presets; you can keep an existing shinyOAuth client if it obtains suitable tokens. A named token target selects the service a token is for, such as "sql" or "storage" in Microsoft’s presets. Set the helper’s target to your client’s name, or use target = NULL for its default token. The Fabric guide has an example.

required_scopes checks permissions before a helper runs. Request those permissions on the OAuth client first; this argument doesn’t request consent or grant database privileges. The source guide lists the scopes its example needs.

For several saved accounts, see vignette("multiple-authorizations", package = "shinyOAuth"). Pass a function such as function() auth$connection(shiny::req(input$authorization_id)) to the database helper. Select IDs from auth$connections(); these identify saved authorizations, separately from token targets.

For another database driver or R package that accepts tokens, see ?oauth_db_connect and ?oauth_db_token.

Recorded backend checks

The table distinguishes real database fixtures from mocked service calls. Versions and results come from the repository’s validation record and integration fixtures, through 9 November 2026. They describe the tested configurations, rather than a list of every supported server version.

Source Checks and versions Coverage limit
CockroachDB CockroachDB 25.4.0, RPostgres 1.4.10 and libpq 16.10; native JWT validation, per-user grants, token replacement and TLS Signed fixture tokens; browser sign-in, live JWKS rotation and CockroachDB Cloud are untested
Native PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 18.3, shared libpq 18 and RPostgres 1.4.10; real Keycloak sign-in, user grants and TLS Native OAuth is tested in Linux containers; Windows uses the unsupported-platform branch
PostgREST PostgREST 16.5 with PostgreSQL 18.3; real sign-in, row policies, writes and TLS Covers the local deployment, not Supabase’s hosted gateway
Trino Trino 484 and RTrino 0.1.0; real JWT sign-in, user grants and TLS A Starburst deployment still needs its own configuration check
SingleStore SingleStore 10.9.0 and Connector/ODBC 1.2.1; JWT validation, per-user grants, bound SQL, dbplyr, reconnects and TLS Signed fixture tokens; browser sign-in, live JWKS rotation and SingleStore Helios are untested
StarRocks StarRocks 3.5.0 and MySQL Connector/ODBC 9.5.0; local JWT sign-in and grants The Docker app is tested; the Windows local-app driver remains unverified
DuckDB over Quack DuckDB 1.5.4; real JWT validation, server policies and TLS The Quack client and server must have compatible versions
libSQL libSQL 0.24.33; real signed tokens, database permissions and HTTPS Hosted Turso external-provider sign-in is not established by this fixture
CrateDB CrateDB 6.4.3; native JWT validation, privileges and HTTPS Uses a local issuer/JWKS gateway
OpenSearch OpenSearch 3.9.0; Security plugin JWT validation, document/field permissions and HTTPS Uses a local signing-key configuration; AWS SigV4 requires another client
Elasticsearch Elasticsearch 9.2.0; native JWT realm, document/field permissions, search, SQL, ES|QL and verified HTTPS Signed fixture tokens; browser sign-in, live JWKS rotation and Elastic Cloud Hosted are untested; Serverless has no JWT realms
ClickHouse Local SQL/HTTPS fixture uses ClickHouse 26.1.2.11 and checks typed parameters and failed write responses The fixture proxy supplies authentication; it does not validate ClickHouse Cloud’s custom-JWT feature
Azure PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 18.3 password fixture, RPostgres 1.4.10 and libpq 16.10; real TLS and recovery after credential replacement Entra token validation and a hosted Azure server are not exercised
Azure MySQL MariaDB Connector/ODBC 3.1.15 and R odbc 1.7.2; local password protocol, 12 KB tokens, credential replacement and verified TLS Entra token validation, Azure user/group mapping and database grants are untested
Databricks brickster 0.2.15 with a MiniLake fixture for DBI/API results, Arrow and pagination MiniLake accepts every token and does not enforce grants; it does not validate Databricks authentication
Fabric and Power BI fabricQueryR 1.0.1 routing, callbacks and generated-app checks Platform calls are mocked; hosted service permissions and native drivers need deployment checks
BigQuery Mocked REST responses cover parameters, polling, pagination, result types and account changes Google browser sign-in, IAM grants and billed query execution are not covered by these mocks
Azure SQL, Snowflake and Redshift R ODBC connection arguments, credential handling and lifecycle tests Real vendor drivers and cloud database authentication remain outside the mocked connection boundary
Supabase, Oracle REST Data Services and Salesforce Mocked HTTP responses and complete app definitions Hosted provider sign-in, server policies and real refresh behavior need configured deployments
SAP HANA and Oracle Database R ODBC boundary, token handling and lifecycle tests; mocked Oracle authentication/context checks No live SAP HANA or Oracle driver/database/provider combination has been validated

Cloud demo browser tests use real Keycloak sign-in with mocked platform operations. They check the local app’s behavior, not the cloud provider’s app registration or data permissions.
